newsitem.title: USA: ADM names G. Allen Andreas president; chairman's nephew.
newsitem.headline: ADM names G. Allen Andreas president; chairman's nephew.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co., which last year pleaded guilty to price-fixing charges, on Monday named G. Allen Andreas, nephew of Chairman Dwayne Andreas, as president.

The move signals a change at the helm of ADM as Allen Andreas, 53, replaces James Randall, who will retire after 29 years with the company, including more than 22 years as president. Allen Andreas was named chief executive officer in April, taking over that title from his uncle.
"Jim Randall has been Dwayne's right-hand man," said Prudential Securities analyst John McMillin. "You basically have a changing of the guard."
The move also highlights the question of when Dwayne Andreas, 79, will step down as chairman and who will some day take over for him.

"It clearly solidifies Allen's position as the chairman-in-waiting," said Jon Lukomnik, New York City deputy controller, who is in charge of several pension funds that own about 3.1 million ADM shares.
But Prudential's McMillin said he did not expect a change in the top spot at ADM any time soon. "I think Dwayne would be chairman as long as Dwayne wants to be," he said.

Dwayne's son, Michael Andreas, who had been vice chairman, was previously considered the heir apparent at ADM. But Michael Andreas and two other former ADM executives face criminal price-fixing charges as part of a Justice Department antitrust investigation.

Michael Andreas; Terrance Wilson, former group vice president in charge of corn refining, and Mark Whitacre, who had been president of ADM's BioProducts Division, have all pleaded not guilty to price-fixing charges.

Last year, ADM pleaded guilty to fixing the prices of lysine, a feed additive, and citric acid, an ingredient in food, beverages and other products. It agreed to pay a record $100 million in criminal fines to the U.S. government.

As president and chief executive officer, Allen Andreas is consolidating operational control at ADM, an agribusiness giant with operations ranging from grain processing and soybean crushing to high-technology food ingredients and vitamins.
"The job of running ADM is huge and complex. Consolidating all that with Allen shows that (he) has to be a very talented and capable person," said Piper Jaffray analyst George Dahlman.

Some institutional shareholders had criticised Allen Andreas' appointment as chief executive officer, since he would be reporting to his uncle, the chairman. In the wake of the antitrust probe, institutional shareholders had sought greater independence between ADM's management and the board.
But those shareholders were more conciliatory toward ADM and Allen Andreas, an executive they see as more open to the concerns of institutional investors than previous regimes.

"We have found him (Allen Andreas) to be a lot more responsive than the previous CEO (Dwayne Andreas)," said Edward Durkin, director of special programmes for the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, which owns about 770,000 ADM shares. "I think we're going to make some positive steps foward this year."

Last month, a federal judge granted preliminary approval of a settlement covering shareholder lawsuits against ADM directors that included payment of $8 million by the directors to the company. As part of that settlement, ADM directors also agreed to adopt certain corporate governance measures, including a new definition of outside director.
"We can make some progress on the board independence standard ... this moves into a phase of active monitoring (of ADM by large shareholders) as opposed to active combat," Durkin said.
ADM's stock was up 37.5 cents at $22.375 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
